paras: The Sardis soldier shooting was a fight at Sardis, Mississippi, in late February or early March 1919, in which a Black soldier recently returned from a training camp shot two white men, Bob Bedford and Barney Nance, after white men interfered in a fight between a white boy and a Black boy. Both men died of their wounds at the Baptist Memorial Hospital in Memphis, and the soldier had not been caught when the reports ran. Black newspapers in several cities reprinted the item as a sign that returned Black soldiers would no longer accept prewar treatment.

According to the only account, the trouble began with a fight between a white boy and "a little Colored boy." When the Black boy got "the best of the scrap," white men interfered, and the soldier went to the boy's rescue. What followed was described as "a pitched battle between the white men and the Colored soldier," in which "the marksmanship of the well trained soldier proved the best."

Bedford and Nance died at the Baptist Memorial Hospital in Memphis in the week before the first report of March 7, and Bedford was said to have had eighteen perforations in his intestines. The account does not give the date of the shooting, the soldier's name, the number of white men involved, or whether anyone else was hurt.

The soldier had "not yet been apprehended," and "from last reports no arrests have been made." A brief printed at the end of March still described him as not apprehended, and no later report of an arrest, inquest or trial appears in the coverage.

The item first appeared in the St. Louis Argus on March 7, 1919, as one paragraph in a front-page column of news about Black soldiers that also covered the death sentence of Sergeant Edgar Caldwell and the Camp Grant courts-martial. On March 22 the Cleveland Advocate ran it under the headline "The Worm Turns!" with a Sardis dateline of March 17, the Phoenix Tribune as "White Man Killed By Colored Soldier Down In Mississippi," and the Wisconsin Weekly Blade, crediting its own news service, as "Resents Brutal Treatment." Each full copy kept the closing comment that "the white people down here are beginning to realize the folly in trying to treat the Colored returned soldiers as they did before the war."

Shorter versions without the account of the fight ran in the Blade on March 29 and the Tribune on April 26, both spelling the first man's name "Medford." None of the Black papers named a source for the story, and none followed it beyond the soldier's escape.

reader.title: Sardis soldier shooting
bases: The only account describes a fight in which white men interfered against a Black boy and a returned Black soldier then shot two of them dead; no Black person is reported killed or hurt and no mob attack is described (A1, A2).
All six Black-press items are copies or condensations of one unattributed report, and no independent account was found (A1, A2, A5).

accounts.label: Black-press news item
accounts.gist: White men interfered when a Black boy was winning a fight with a white boy; a Black soldier back from training camp came to the boy's rescue and outshot them in a 'pitched battle', killing two; he had not been caught and no arrests were made.

framing.detail: The Cleveland Advocate headed the item 'The Worm Turns!' and every full copy closed with the remark that 'the white people down here' were learning 'the folly' of treating returned Black soldiers as before the war, presenting the shooting as resistance rather than crime.
The Wisconsin Weekly Blade headed its copy 'Resents Brutal Treatment'; the Phoenix Tribune's headline, 'White Man Killed By Colored Soldier Down In Mississippi', stated the outcome plainly.

conflicts.note: The full copies, including the earliest, print Bedford; the later condensed briefs print Medford, likely a typesetting variant. 'Barnnew' in A1 is OCR or a misprint for Barney.
